name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
title: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
answer: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the use of AI to identify competing readings of a statute, model how a court or regulator might resolve ambiguity, and surface arguments that favor one side in litigation or compliance disputes. It covers federal and state statutes, administrative rules, and local ordinances where language is contested. The page focuses on tools and workflows that help lawyers test interpretive theories before filing briefs or responding to enforcement actions.

sections.body: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the use of AI to identify competing readings of a statute, model how a court or regulator might resolve ambiguity, and surface arguments that favor one side in litigation or compliance disputes. It covers federal and state statutes, administrative rules, and local ordinances where language is contested. The page focuses on tools and workflows that help lawyers test interpretive theories before filing briefs or responding to enforcement actions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on large language models fine-tuned on statutory text, legislative history, and judicial opinions, often combined with retrieval over case law databases and regulatory dockets. Many deployments use private cloud instances so that privileged case strategy does not leave the firm's control. The site's tracking of 6823 state AI bills and 210 compliance pages provides a live corpus for testing how new statutory language is being drafted and contested.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by prompting or training models to generate plausible interpretations, then using counter-models or adversarial prompts to attack those interpretations. Lawyers compare the outputs against canons of construction, such as textualism or purposivism, and against the record of how similar language has been treated in prior cases. The output is not a single answer but a ranked set of arguments, weaknesses, and likely judicial responses.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on the provenance of training data and the danger of hallucinated legislative history or fabricated case citations. A lawyer must verify every quoted statute, committee report, and precedent before relying on it, because the model may conflate jurisdictions or invent amendments. Confidentiality is also a risk if a public model is used, so many firms require on-premises or contractual isolation. The site's 29 AI case law precedents and 142 active AI lawsuits include disputes over AI-generated legal work, which shape the duty of competence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward specialized statutory interpreters that can track how a single phrase has been construed across all 50 states and federal circuits in near real time. Future tools may simulate oral argument or predict the effect of a proposed amendment on pending litigation. As state legislatures add thousands of AI-related bills each year, the ability to compare adversarial readings quickly will become a standard part of case strategy rather than a novelty.
